title: Belowground podcast: Digital droplet PCR to estimate root biomass and species profiling from soil samples
content: Plant roots play a crucial role in nutrient uptake, carbon cycling, and interactions with soil microbiota, yet they remain challenging to study due to their hidden nature (Freschet et al. 2021). Traditional methods for root biomass estimation, such as soil coring, washing, and dry-weight analysis, are labor intensive, destructive, and often lack taxonomic resolution, especially in mixed-species systems (Bardgett et al. 2014). Recent advances in molecular techniques, particularly those targeting plant-specific nucleic acid sequences, offer a nondestructive and scalable means for identifying plant roots in complex soil environments. Among these, quantitative PCR (qPCR) has been used for species-specific detection in root samples, providing a nonmorphological approach to species identification (Mommer et al. 2011). The qPCR relies on fluorescence-based, real-time quantification of nucleic acid from a sample. Despite being conceptually simple and practical, it has limitations, including reduced sensitivity and quantification accuracy in complex or degraded samples, and vulnerability to PCR inhibitors commonly found in soil nucleic acid extracts (Bustin et al. 2009; Smith and Osborn 2009).
